Immaterial

im-uh-TEER-ee-ul -- stress on the third syllable, TEER. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Immaterial is unimportant or irrelevant.

Whether the vase was a gift or a purchase is immaterial; either way, it belongs to her now.

Worked Example

During a school-board debate about whether the day should start an hour later, one speaker spends two full minutes on the cafeteria's terrible pizza.

The pizza complaint is immaterial: it may be perfectly true, yet it has nothing to do with the question being decided. Immaterial does not call a fact false -- it calls it beside the point.

How Immaterial Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

irrelevant

irrelevant: not connected with the matter at hand

unimportant

unimportant: of little significance

inconsequential

inconsequential: too small to have any effect on the outcome

Antonyms

relevant

relevant: directly connected to the matter at hand

pertinent

pertinent: directly related and genuinely useful to the question

How Strong Is It? — unimportant → immaterial → irrelevant

unimportant vs. immaterial

unimportant vs. immaterial: Unimportant is the plain, general word -- an unimportant detail matters little -- while immaterial goes further and says the detail has no bearing whatever on the decision.

irrelevant vs. immaterial

irrelevant vs. immaterial: Irrelevant is the sharper cousin of immaterial: immaterial says a fact does not affect the outcome, while irrelevant says it does not even belong in the conversation.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — im-

prefix — im-: not (the form in- takes before m) (Latin in-)

root — material

root — material: made of matter; substantial, and so significant (Latin materia 'matter, substance')

Put it together

Put it together: Immaterial is this unit's prefix in its im- form (in- becomes im- before m) attached to material, a complete English word. Literally it means 'not made of matter' -- and that older sense still exists for ghosts and spirits. The everyday sense grew out of it by metaphor: a point with no substance behind it carries no weight in an argument, so it is immaterial.

Use the root in a new word: materialize

Use the root in a new word: materialize: The promised funding never materialized, and the project quietly ended.

Root Check

Word Choice

Immaterial lives in arguments, courtrooms, and debates: 'that is immaterial to the case,' 'the delay is immaterial.' It keeps a second, older meaning -- 'not made of physical matter,' as in an immaterial spirit -- but the sense the ISEE tests is 'irrelevant, does not matter.'
